sourceFact.title: Desert Arch
sourceFact.fact: A desert arch forms when softer rock wears away over time, leaving a curved opening in harder rock.
sourceFact.food: This scene features a tall rock arch, dry desert ground, bright sunlight, and open blue sky.
sourceFact.stronghold: Natural rock arches are common in dry sandstone regions such as the American Southwest and other desert landscapes.
learningPoints: Wind, rain, freezing, and heat can slowly shape desert rocks.
Many arches take thousands or millions of years to form.
Desert plants and animals survive with very little water.

sourceFact.title: Golden Grass at Sunset
sourceFact.fact: At sunset, sunlight passes through more of the atmosphere, often making grasses glow in warm gold, orange, or red tones.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows tall grass stems, warm sunset light, and a peaceful outdoor field.
sourceFact.stronghold: Golden sunset grasslands can be seen in fields, meadows, prairies, and countryside areas around the world.
learningPoints: Grasslands provide homes and food for many insects, birds, and mammals.
The Sun appears lower in the sky during sunrise and sunset.
Backlighting can make thin grass stems look bright and glowing.

sourceFact.title: Spring Blossoms
sourceFact.fact: Spring blossoms are flowers that open on trees and shrubs when warmer weather and longer daylight return.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows soft pink blossoms, small branches, and gentle spring light.
sourceFact.stronghold: Blossoming trees are found in gardens, parks, orchards, and forests in many temperate regions.
learningPoints: Many fruit trees bloom before they grow fruit.
Bees and other pollinators visit blossoms for nectar and pollen.
Spring flowers are often a sign that plants are starting a new growing season.

sourceFact.title: Rolling Hills
sourceFact.fact: Rolling hills are gently rising and falling landforms shaped by weathering, water, wind, and long-term changes in the landscape.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows green hills, open countryside, and a peaceful natural landscape.
sourceFact.stronghold: Rolling hills are common in rural areas, grasslands, farming regions, and foothills around the world.
learningPoints: Hills are lower and usually less steep than mountains.
Grass-covered hills can support grazing animals and wildflowers.
Sunlight and shadows can make hill shapes easier to see.

sourceFact.title: Bald Eagle
sourceFact.fact: The bald eagle is a large bird of prey known for its white head, strong hooked beak, and powerful eyesight.
sourceFact.food: Bald eagles mainly eat fish, but they may also eat birds, small mammals, and carrion.
sourceFact.stronghold: Bald eagles live in North America, often near lakes, rivers, coasts, and wetlands.
learningPoints: Bald eagles build very large nests high in trees or on cliffs.
Their sharp talons help them catch and hold prey.
They are a national symbol of the United States.

sourceFact.title: Mountain Road
sourceFact.fact: Mountain roads often wind through valleys and passes because steep rocky terrain makes straight roads difficult to build.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows a road leading toward high peaks, open sky, and rugged mountain scenery.
sourceFact.stronghold: Mountain roads are found in ranges such as the Rockies, Alps, Andes, Himalayas, and many other highland regions.
learningPoints: Mountains can create changing weather and cooler temperatures.
Roads through mountains may follow valleys or natural gaps.
Snow, ice, and rockfall can make mountain travel challenging.

sourceFact.title: Desert Rock Formations
sourceFact.fact: Desert rock formations are shaped over long periods by erosion from wind, rain, temperature changes, and moving sand.
sourceFact.food: This scene features layered rocks, dry ground, warm sunlight, and open desert space.
sourceFact.stronghold: These formations are common in dry regions with exposed sandstone, limestone, or volcanic rock.
learningPoints: Different rock layers can show different periods of Earth’s history.
Desert landscapes can be very hot in the day and cold at night.
Erosion slowly changes cliffs, towers, arches, and canyons.

sourceFact.title: Northern Lights
sourceFact.fact: The northern lights are glowing colors in the sky caused when charged particles from space interact with gases in Earth’s atmosphere.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows colorful night-sky lights, dark land, and a dramatic Arctic-style landscape.
sourceFact.stronghold: Northern lights are most often seen near the Arctic, including places such as Alaska, Canada, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and Finland.
learningPoints: Northern lights are also called aurora borealis.
They are easier to see on dark, clear nights away from city lights.
Auroras can appear green, purple, pink, red, or blue.

sourceFact.title: Shorebird
sourceFact.fact: Shorebirds are birds that often feed along beaches, mudflats, wetlands, and shallow water edges.
sourceFact.food: Many shorebirds eat insects, worms, small crustaceans, and tiny creatures found in sand or mud.
sourceFact.stronghold: Shorebirds are found along coasts, lakeshores, rivers, and wetlands across many parts of the world.
learningPoints: Long legs help many shorebirds walk through shallow water.
Some shorebirds have long beaks for probing mud and sand.
Many shorebirds migrate long distances between breeding and feeding areas.

sourceFact.title: Spotted Gecko
sourceFact.fact: Geckos are small reptiles, and many species use spotted or patterned skin to blend into rocks, bark, or sandy ground.
sourceFact.food: Most geckos eat insects and other small invertebrates.
sourceFact.stronghold: Geckos live in warm regions around the world, including deserts, forests, grasslands, and homes.
learningPoints: Many geckos are active at night.
Some geckos can climb smooth surfaces using special toe pads.
A gecko may drop its tail to escape a predator, and some can regrow it.

sourceFact.title: Flying Goose
sourceFact.fact: Geese are strong flying birds that often travel in groups and may form a V-shape during long migrations.
sourceFact.food: Geese eat grasses, grains, aquatic plants, seeds, and sometimes small insects.
sourceFact.stronghold: Geese are found near lakes, wetlands, fields, rivers, and coastlines across many regions of the world.
learningPoints: Flying in a V formation can help geese save energy.
Geese communicate with loud honking calls.
Many geese return to the same nesting or feeding areas each year.

sourceFact.title: Tabby Cat
sourceFact.fact: A tabby cat has striped, spotted, or swirled coat markings, often with an M-shaped mark on the forehead.
sourceFact.food: Cats are meat-eaters and need animal protein in their diet.
sourceFact.stronghold: Domestic cats live with people around the world in homes, farms, neighborhoods, and cities.
learningPoints: Cats use whiskers to sense nearby objects and spaces.
Their ears can turn to help locate tiny sounds.
Cats groom their fur with rough tongues.

sourceFact.title: Poppy Meadow
sourceFact.fact: A poppy meadow is a field where bright poppy flowers grow among grasses and other plants.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows vivid red poppies, green stems, open meadow space, and sunlight.
sourceFact.stronghold: Poppies grow in fields, meadows, gardens, and disturbed soils in many temperate regions.
learningPoints: Poppies often have thin, delicate petals.
Flowers attract pollinators such as bees and butterflies.
Meadows can support many insects, birds, and small animals.

sourceFact.title: Orb Weaver Spider
sourceFact.fact: Orb-weaver spiders are known for building round, wheel-shaped webs that help catch flying insects.
sourceFact.food: Orb-weaver spiders eat insects that become trapped in their sticky webs.
sourceFact.stronghold: Orb-weaver spiders are found in gardens, forests, fields, and around buildings in many parts of the world.
learningPoints: Many orb webs have a spiral pattern.
Spiders use silk to build webs, wrap prey, and make egg sacs.
Spiders have eight legs and are arachnids, not insects.

sourceFact.title: Great Wall
sourceFact.fact: The Great Wall is a long system of walls, watchtowers, and fortifications built across parts of northern China over many centuries.
sourceFact.food: It is famous for its long stone pathways, mountain views, and historic watchtowers.
sourceFact.stronghold: The Great Wall is in northern China, with famous restored sections near Beijing.
learningPoints: Different Chinese dynasties built and repaired different sections.
Some parts of the wall cross steep hills and mountains.
The wall is one of the most recognized landmarks in the world.

sourceFact.title: Alpine Village
sourceFact.fact: An alpine village is a settlement in or near high mountain regions, often surrounded by peaks, forests, lakes, or meadows.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows a mountain village, green slopes, water, and bright alpine scenery.
sourceFact.stronghold: Alpine villages are common in mountain regions such as the Alps, but similar villages exist in many highland areas worldwide.
learningPoints: Mountain villages often adapt to snow, steep slopes, and cooler weather.
Lakes and valleys can form from glaciers and mountain streams.
Tourism, farming, and local crafts are important in many alpine communities.

sourceFact.title: Yellow Dahlia
sourceFact.fact: Dahlias are flowering plants known for bold, layered blooms that can come in many shapes, sizes, and colors.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows a bright yellow dahlia bloom with many detailed petals.
sourceFact.stronghold: Dahlias are grown in gardens and flower farms around the world, and they originally come from Mexico and Central America.
learningPoints: Dahlia flowers can have many rows of petals.
They are popular garden flowers because of their bright colors.
Pollinators such as bees may visit dahlia blooms.

sourceFact.title: Butterfly on Bloom
sourceFact.fact: Butterflies often visit flowers to sip nectar using a long, tube-like mouthpart called a proboscis.
sourceFact.food: Adult butterflies mostly drink nectar, while caterpillars usually eat leaves from host plants.
sourceFact.stronghold: Butterflies live in meadows, gardens, forests, wetlands, and many other habitats around the world.
learningPoints: Butterflies go through metamorphosis from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to adult.
Their wings are covered with tiny scales.
Butterflies help pollinate some flowers as they move from bloom to bloom.

sourceFact.title: Orange Butterfly on Thistle
sourceFact.fact: Orange butterflies often rest on nectar-rich flowers such as thistles, using their delicate legs and curled feeding tube.
sourceFact.food: Butterflies drink nectar from flowers, while their caterpillars feed on specific host plants.
sourceFact.stronghold: Butterflies and thistles can be found in gardens, meadows, roadsides, and wildflower areas in many regions.
learningPoints: Thistle flowers can provide nectar for bees, butterflies, and other insects.
Butterfly wing colors and patterns can help with camouflage or warning signals.
Butterflies are important parts of many food webs.

sourceFact.title: Waterfall in a Misty Jungle
sourceFact.fact: A waterfall forms where a river drops over a steep rock edge or cliff.
sourceFact.food: This scene features falling water, misty air, lush plants, and a green valley.
sourceFact.stronghold: Waterfalls are found worldwide, especially in mountainous and rainy regions.
learningPoints: Mist from waterfalls can help nearby plants stay moist.
Fast-moving water can slowly shape the rocks below.
Jungle valleys often support many kinds of plants and animals.

sourceFact.title: Aurora Over Icy Lagoon
sourceFact.fact: An aurora is a glowing light display in the sky created when particles from space interact with Earth’s atmosphere.
sourceFact.food: This scene is known for colorful night skies, icy water, and reflections on the lagoon.
sourceFact.stronghold: Auroras are most common near the Arctic and Antarctic regions, including Iceland, Norway, and Canada.
learningPoints: Auroras can appear green, pink, purple, and red.
They are easier to see on dark, clear nights.
The same natural event is called aurora borealis in the north and aurora australis in the south.

images.sourceTitle: Stormy Waves on a Rugged Coast

sourceFact.title: Stormy Waves on a Rugged Coast
sourceFact.fact: Powerful ocean waves can crash against rocky shores and reshape coastlines over time.
sourceFact.food: This scene features rough seas, dark clouds, and rocky cliffs along the shore.
sourceFact.stronghold: Stormy coastlines are common in windy ocean regions such as the North Atlantic and the Southern Ocean.
learningPoints: Strong storms can make waves much larger than usual.
Rocky coasts are worn down little by little by water and wind.
Sea spray can travel far inland during rough weather.

sourceFact.title: Glowing Mangrove Bay
sourceFact.fact: Some bays glow at night because tiny living organisms in the water create bioluminescent light.
sourceFact.food: This scene includes glowing water, mangrove trees, and a sky full of stars.
sourceFact.stronghold: Bioluminescent bays are found in places such as Puerto Rico and some tropical coastal regions.
learningPoints: Mangroves grow along salty coasts and help protect shorelines.
Bioluminescence is light made by living things.
The glow often becomes brighter when the water is disturbed.

sourceFact.title: Sunlight Through Canyon Walls
sourceFact.fact: Canyons are deep valleys cut by rivers or floods over long periods of time.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows narrow rock walls, warm sunlight beams, and smooth canyon curves.
sourceFact.stronghold: Beautiful canyons are found in many dry regions, including the United States, Jordan, and Australia.
learningPoints: Sunlight can create glowing colors on canyon walls.
Flash floods can help carve narrow canyon passages.
Different rock layers can show Earth’s history over time.

images.sourceTitle: Giant Trees in a Rocky Desert

sourceFact.title: Giant Trees in a Rocky Desert
sourceFact.fact: Some hardy trees can survive in dry places with little rain by storing water and growing deep roots.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows giant trees, dry rocky ground, and wide open desert skies.
sourceFact.stronghold: Tree-filled desert landscapes can be found in places such as Socotra, Namibia, and the American Southwest.
learningPoints: Desert plants often grow slowly and conserve water carefully.
Rocks and sand can become extremely hot during the day.
Even dry landscapes can support unique life forms.

sourceFact.title: Sandstone Pillars in Mist
sourceFact.fact: Sandstone pillars are tall rock formations shaped over time by wind, rain, and changing temperatures.
sourceFact.food: This scene shows steep rock pillars, misty air, and a green forested valley.
sourceFact.stronghold: Towering sandstone formations are found in places such as China, the United States, and parts of Europe.
learningPoints: Sandstone forms from layers of sand pressed together over a very long time.
Mist can make distant cliffs look softer and more mysterious.
Erosion slowly changes rock shapes over thousands of years.

sourceFact.title: Geothermal Springs
sourceFact.fact: Geothermal springs are heated by warm energy from deep inside the Earth.
sourceFact.food: This scene features steaming water, mineral-rich pools, and surrounding forest views.
sourceFact.stronghold: Geothermal springs are common in places with volcanic activity, such as Iceland, New Zealand, and Yellowstone in the United States.
learningPoints: Some springs bubble because hot water and gases rise to the surface.
Minerals can color the water and rocks in surprising shades.
These areas can be very hot, so people should stay on safe paths.

sourceFact.title: Mirror of the Fiery Sky
sourceFact.fact: Still water can reflect a colorful sunrise or sunset so clearly that it looks like a mirror.
sourceFact.food: This scene is known for calm water, dramatic sky colors, and bright reflections.
sourceFact.stronghold: These reflections can happen anywhere there is still water and a vivid sky.
learningPoints: Red and orange skies often appear when sunlight travels through more of the atmosphere.
Wind can break up a reflection by making waves.
Reflections are easier to see on smooth water than on rough water.

sourceFact.title: Cascading Terraces
sourceFact.fact: Terraces are step-like levels built on hillsides to manage water and make farming easier.
sourceFact.food: This scene is known for layered slopes, shining water, and warm golden tones.
sourceFact.stronghold: Terraced landscapes are found in countries such as China, Vietnam, Peru, and the Philippines.
learningPoints: Terraces help keep soil from washing away.
They can hold water for crops like rice.
Sunlight can make terraced fields glow beautifully at sunrise or sunset.

sourceFact.title: Clownfish
sourceFact.fact: Clownfish are small, bright fish famous for living safely among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones.
sourceFact.food: Clownfish eat algae, plankton, and tiny sea animals.
sourceFact.stronghold: Clownfish live in warm waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
learningPoints: A special mucus on their skin helps protect them from anemone stings.
They are usually orange with white stripes.
Clownfish and sea anemones help each other survive.

sourceFact.title: Dolphin
sourceFact.fact: Dolphins are smart marine mammals that breathe air and often live in social groups called pods.
sourceFact.food: Dolphins eat fish, squid, and other small sea animals.
sourceFact.stronghold: Many dolphins live in warm and temperate oceans around the world, with large populations in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
learningPoints: Dolphins come to the surface to breathe through a blowhole.
They use clicks and whistles to communicate and find food.
Dolphins are mammals, so mothers feed milk to their babies.

sourceFact.title: Jellyfish
sourceFact.fact: Jellyfish have soft, umbrella-shaped bodies and trailing tentacles that drift through the water.
sourceFact.food: Jellyfish eat tiny fish, plankton, and other small sea creatures.
sourceFact.stronghold: Jellyfish live in oceans all over the world, from shallow coasts to deep sea waters.
learningPoints: Some jellyfish glow in the dark ocean with bioluminescence.
Their tentacles can sting to help catch food.
Jellyfish have no bones, brain, or heart.

sourceFact.title: Lionfish
sourceFact.fact: Lionfish are striking reef fish with long, fan-like spines and bold stripes.
sourceFact.food: Lionfish eat small fish and crustaceans.
sourceFact.stronghold: Lionfish are native to the Indo-Pacific region, though they are also found in other waters as an invasive species.
learningPoints: Their spines contain venom for defense.
Lionfish often move slowly and hunt by surprising prey.
Their dramatic fins help them look larger to predators.

sourceFact.title: Manta Ray
sourceFact.fact: Manta rays are large, graceful sea animals with wide fins that look like underwater wings.
sourceFact.food: Manta rays mainly eat plankton and tiny sea animals.
sourceFact.stronghold: Manta rays are found in tropical and subtropical oceans around the world.
learningPoints: They glide through the water with smooth, powerful movements.
Manta rays do not have the stinging tail seen in some other rays.
They often visit coral reefs and cleaning stations.

sourceFact.title: Octopus
sourceFact.fact: Octopuses are clever sea animals with eight arms and strong suckers.
sourceFact.food: Octopuses eat crabs, shellfish, and other small sea creatures.
sourceFact.stronghold: Octopuses live in oceans all over the world, often hiding in reefs and rocky seafloors.
learningPoints: An octopus can squeeze through very small spaces.
It can change color to help hide from predators.
Octopuses are known for problem-solving skills.

sourceFact.title: Sea Turtle
sourceFact.fact: Sea turtles are reptiles that spend most of their lives in the ocean but come onto beaches to lay eggs.
sourceFact.food: Different sea turtles eat seagrass, jellyfish, crabs, and other sea life.
sourceFact.stronghold: Sea turtles live in warm and temperate oceans, with important nesting beaches in countries such as Australia, Costa Rica, and Oman.
learningPoints: Sea turtles can travel very long distances in the ocean.
Their flippers help them swim strongly through the water.
Many baby turtles hatch on beaches and head to the sea on their own.

sourceFact.title: Seahorse
sourceFact.fact: Seahorses are tiny fish that swim upright and use their curled tails to hold onto plants or coral.
sourceFact.food: Seahorses eat tiny shrimp-like animals and plankton.
sourceFact.stronghold: Seahorses live in shallow tropical and temperate waters around the world.
learningPoints: A seahorse uses its long snout like a straw to suck up food.
Male seahorses carry the babies in a pouch.
They are not strong swimmers and often drift with the water.

sourceFact.title: Starfish
sourceFact.fact: Starfish, also called sea stars, are marine animals that usually have five arms.
sourceFact.food: Sea stars often eat shellfish and tiny sea animals.
sourceFact.stronghold: Sea stars live in oceans worldwide, from coral reefs to rocky shores.
learningPoints: A sea star can move using tiny tube feet underneath its body.
Some sea stars can regrow a lost arm.
They are not actually fish.

sourceFact.title: Whale
sourceFact.fact: Whales are giant marine mammals that travel through oceans and come to the surface to breathe air.
sourceFact.food: Different whales eat krill, plankton, fish, or squid depending on the species.
sourceFact.stronghold: Whales are found in every ocean, with many species migrating across huge distances each year.
learningPoints: Some whales are the largest animals on Earth.
Whales use sounds to communicate over long distances underwater.
Like all mammals, whales breathe air and care for their young.

sourceFact.title: Whale
sourceFact.fact: Whales are giant marine mammals that travel through oceans and come to the surface to breathe air.
sourceFact.food: Different whales eat krill, plankton, fish, or squid depending on the species.
sourceFact.stronghold: Whales are found in every ocean, with many species migrating across huge distances each year.
learningPoints: Some whales are the largest animals on Earth.
Whales use sounds to communicate over long distances underwater.
Like all mammals, whales breathe air and care for their young.

sourceFact.title: Rough Seawall Waves
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows waves breaking beside a seawall and wooden posts.
sourceFact.food: Coasts are where land meets the ocean, and waves, tides, wind, and erosion constantly reshape the shoreline.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for waves breaking beside a seawall and wooden posts.
learningPoints: Waves can slowly carve cliffs, beaches, and rocky shores.
Tides change how much shoreline is covered by water.
Coastal habitats support birds, fish, shellfish, and many small animals.

sourceFact.title: Sea Lion on the Beach
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a sea lion resting on a sandy beach near the surf.
sourceFact.food: Sea lions are marine mammals that breathe air, rest on land, and swim powerfully through coastal waters.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a sea lion resting on a sandy beach near the surf.
learningPoints: Sea lions come to the surface to breathe air.
Their flippers help them move on land and swim in the ocean.
They often rest on beaches, docks, or rocks between feeding trips.

sourceFact.title: Blue Reef Bubbles
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows blue bubbles and rounded underwater shapes clustered like a reef garden.
sourceFact.food: Reefs are busy underwater habitats that support many different plants and animals.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for blue bubbles and rounded underwater shapes clustered like a reef garden.
learningPoints: Reefs are full of hiding places for small animals.
Bright colors can warn, attract, or camouflage reef creatures.
Healthy reefs depend on clean water and balanced ecosystems.

sourceFact.title: Sea Lion Portrait
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a close view of a sea lion with smooth whiskers and wet fur.
sourceFact.food: Sea lions are marine mammals that breathe air, rest on land, and swim powerfully through coastal waters.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a close view of a sea lion with smooth whiskers and wet fur.

Their flippers help them move on land and swim in the ocean.

sourceFact.title: Coastal Cliff Bay
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows green coastal cliffs curving around calm ocean water.
sourceFact.food: Coasts are where land meets the ocean, and waves, tides, wind, and erosion constantly reshape the shoreline.

learningPoints: Waves can slowly carve cliffs, beaches, and rocky shores.
Tides change how much shoreline is covered by water.
Coastal habitats support birds, fish, shellfish, and many small animals.

sourceFact.title: Seal in the Water
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a seal head peeking above blue ocean water.
sourceFact.food: Seals are marine mammals that breathe air and use streamlined bodies to swim through cold ocean water.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a seal head peeking above blue ocean water.
learningPoints: Seals use streamlined bodies and flippers to swim efficiently.
They can hold their breath while diving for food.
Many seals rest on beaches, ice, or rocks after swimming.

sourceFact.title: Dolphin Pool Moment
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a dolphin rising from bright blue water near a pool edge.
sourceFact.food: Dolphins are intelligent marine mammals that breathe through blowholes and often live in social groups.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a dolphin rising from bright blue water near a pool edge.
learningPoints: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole.
They use clicks and whistles to communicate and find food.
Dolphin groups are called pods.

sourceFact.title: Shorebird Resting
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a speckled shorebird resting beside rippled water.
sourceFact.food: Seabirds are birds adapted to life near oceans, beaches, cliffs, and coastal feeding areas.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a speckled shorebird resting beside rippled water.
learningPoints: Many seabirds feed on fish and other small ocean animals.
Long wings help some seabirds glide over water.
Coasts provide nesting, resting, and feeding places.

sourceFact.title: Sailboats on the Horizon
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows small sailboats moving across a calm blue sea.
sourceFact.food: Boats help people travel, fish, explore, and study coastal and ocean environments.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for small sailboats moving across a calm blue sea.
learningPoints: Boats need safe weather, navigation, and awareness of currents.
Small boats can show scale in wide ocean scenes.
Harbors and bays often protect boats from rough waves.

sourceFact.title: Sea Anemone on Reef
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a pale sea anemone growing from a colorful reef surface.
sourceFact.food: Sea anemones are ocean animals with tentacles that can provide shelter for some reef creatures.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a pale sea anemone growing from a colorful reef surface.
learningPoints: Sea anemones use tentacles to catch tiny drifting animals.
Some fish can live safely among anemone tentacles.
Anemones are animals, even though they look like flowers.

sourceFact.title: Red Shore Crab
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a red crab walking across a sandy or rocky beach.
sourceFact.food: Crabs are crustaceans with hard shells, jointed legs, and claws used for feeding and defense.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a red crab walking across a sandy or rocky beach.
learningPoints: Crabs have hard outer shells called exoskeletons.
Many crabs walk sideways using jointed legs.
Crabs help clean beaches and shallow seafloors by eating many kinds of food.

sourceFact.title: Gull Skimming Water
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a gull flying low over rippled ocean water.
sourceFact.food: Seabirds are birds adapted to life near oceans, beaches, cliffs, and coastal feeding areas.

learningPoints: Many seabirds feed on fish and other small ocean animals.
Long wings help some seabirds glide over water.

sourceFact.title: Seagull on Rock Wall
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a seagull standing on a rough stone wall by the water.
sourceFact.food: Seabirds are birds adapted to life near oceans, beaches, cliffs, and coastal feeding areas.

learningPoints: Many seabirds feed on fish and other small ocean animals.
Long wings help some seabirds glide over water.
Coasts provide nesting, resting, and feeding places.

sourceFact.title: Blue Glacier Face
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a blue-white glacier wall meeting cold ocean water.
sourceFact.food: Glaciers near the ocean are huge moving masses of ice that can break into floating pieces called icebergs.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a blue-white glacier wall meeting cold ocean water.
learningPoints: Glacier ice can look blue when it absorbs other colors of light.
Pieces of glacier ice can break off into the sea.
Cold coastal waters near glaciers can support specialized wildlife.

sourceFact.title: Beach Gull at Sunset
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a gull standing on a beach in warm sunset light.

sourceFact.title: Shallow Reef Creature
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a dark sea creature resting among green underwater plants and reef textures.
sourceFact.food: Reef animals use camouflage, color, texture, and shelter to survive in crowded underwater habitats.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a dark sea creature resting among green underwater plants and reef textures.
learningPoints: Textures and colors help reef animals blend in or stand out.
Many reef creatures hide among plants, rocks, and coral.
Reef habitats are crowded with many species living close together.

sourceFact.title: Flying Seagull
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a white seabird flying across a clear blue sky.
sourceFact.food: Seabirds are birds adapted to life near oceans, beaches, cliffs, and coastal feeding areas.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a white seabird flying across a clear blue sky.
learningPoints: Many seabirds feed on fish and other small ocean animals.
Long wings help some seabirds glide over water.
Coasts provide nesting, resting, and feeding places.

sourceFact.title: Swimming Sea Turtle
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a sea turtle swimming through blue-green underwater light.
sourceFact.food: Sea turtles are ocean reptiles that breathe air and travel long distances through marine habitats.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a sea turtle swimming through blue-green underwater light.
learningPoints: Sea turtles breathe air but spend most of their lives in the ocean.
Their flippers help them swim long distances.
Many sea turtles return to sandy beaches to lay eggs.

sourceFact.title: Swimming Sharks
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows several sharks moving together through deep blue water.
sourceFact.food: Sharks are fish with cartilage skeletons, strong senses, and important roles in ocean food webs.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for several sharks moving together through deep blue water.
learningPoints: Sharks have skeletons made of cartilage instead of bone.
Many sharks use powerful senses to find food.
Sharks help keep ocean ecosystems balanced.

sourceFact.title: Spiny Lobster
sourceFact.fact: This ocean image shows a spiny lobster tucked among reddish reef rocks.
sourceFact.food: Spiny lobsters are crustaceans with long antennae and hard protective shells.
sourceFact.stronghold: Look for a spiny lobster tucked among reddish reef rocks.
learningPoints: Spiny lobsters have long antennae instead of large front claws.
Their hard shells protect their bodies.

Layered clothing helps people stay warm in freezing weather.

sourceFact.title: Rainy Umbrella

It is the last surviving wonder of the ancient world.

sourceFact.title: Great Wall of China
sourceFact.fact: The Great Wall is a huge system of walls and watchtowers built over many centuries in China.
sourceFact.food: It is famous for its long stone pathways, mountain views, and history of guarding ancient borders.
sourceFact.stronghold: The Great Wall is in northern China, with famous restored sections near Beijing.
learningPoints: It is one of the most famous landmarks in the world.
Different dynasties added new parts over time.
Some sections climb steep hills and mountains.

sourceFact.title: Machu Picchu
sourceFact.fact: Machu Picchu is an ancient Inca site high in the Andes Mountains.
sourceFact.food: It is famous for its stone terraces, mountain setting, and Inca history.
sourceFact.stronghold: Machu Picchu is in Peru near Cusco.
learningPoints: The site sits high above a river valley.
The Inca built strong stone walls without modern machines.
It stayed hidden from much of the outside world for a long time.

sourceFact.title: Petra
sourceFact.fact: Petra is an ancient city famous for buildings carved directly into pink rock cliffs.
sourceFact.food: It is famous for rock-cut architecture, narrow canyons, and desert history.
sourceFact.stronghold: Petra is in southern Jordan.
learningPoints: Petra is sometimes called the Rose City because of its stone color.
People enter through a narrow canyon called the Siq.
It was an important trading city long ago.

sourceFact.title: Taj Mahal
sourceFact.fact: The Taj Mahal is a white marble monument built in India and known for its beautiful symmetry.
sourceFact.food: It is famous for its shining marble, detailed carvings, and reflecting pools.
sourceFact.stronghold: The Taj Mahal stands in Agra, India, on the banks of the Yamuna River.
learningPoints: It was built as a mausoleum.
The marble can look different colors at different times of day.
It is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
